cards.title: SN2 mechanism: four marks for exact arrows, not just the idea

walkthrough.question: Bromoalkane X is CH3CHBrC(CH3)3. It reacts with sodium hydroxide, and the reaction depends on the concentrations of both reactants. Using curly arrows to show how the electrons move, explain the mechanism of this reaction. [4]
walkthrough.key_idea: Rate depends on both reactants, so SN2: one step, two arrows, one charged transition state.
walkthrough.question_type: Draw SN2 mechanism with curly arrows
walkthrough.careful: Start the first arrow on oxygen's lone pair, never on H.
procedure: Decide SN2 or SN1 from the rate clue.
Draw arrow from lone pair on O of OH⁻ to C.
Draw arrow from the C–Br bond to Br.
Draw the transition state: partial bonds, overall negative charge.
Write the products: the alcohol and Br⁻.
tricks: Check charge: OH⁻ in, one minus in transition state, Br⁻ out.
Ignore Na⁺: start the arrow from OH⁻, not NaOH.
HO and Br need not sit at 180°; do not redraw.
if_lost: Does the stem say the rate depends on one reactant or both?
Which atom in the hydroxide ion carries the lone pair?
Which carbon is slightly positive, and why?
Where do the electrons in the breaking bond end up?

1_context.short: Secondary bromide; the rate clue points to SN2.
1_context.why: Secondary halogenoalkanes can react by both mechanisms, so structure alone cannot decide. The concentration clue does.
1_context.avoid: Deciding from structure alone: secondary allows either mechanism, and an SN1 answer caps at 3 marks here.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.9: primary SN2, tertiary SN1, both for secondary; describe and explain the mechanisms.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show SN2 on a small primary molecule. This question uses a bulky secondary bromide and hides the choice in the stem.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Four marks: two arrows, transition state, products.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Each mark checks a separate feature of electron movement, so a correct name alone earns nothing and one slip costs only one mark.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Arrow from the H of OH⁻, or from C instead of the C–Br bond, both reported repeatedly (11M.2.HL.TZ2.8, 17M.2.HL.TZ2.7).
trigger_phrases: arrow from lone pair/negative charge on O to C bonded to Br
arrow from C–Br bond to Br
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: An SN1 mechanism caps at 3 marks. NaBr as a product counts only if Na⁺ was shown at the start.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Full credit needs both transition-state features and both products. Partial bonds without the charge, or a missing Br⁻, loses that mark.

3_novel_application.short: Bulky X looks odd, but only one carbon matters.
3_novel_application.why: The mechanism happens at the carbon holding Br, so the rest of the molecule is carried through unchanged as an R group.
3_novel_application.avoid: Miscopying the C(CH3)3 end; examiners saw wrong organic products on this question (25M.2.HL.6221.4).
3_novel_application.disguise: A bulky C(CH3)3 group replaces the usual small primary bromide.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Circle C–Br, call the rest R, then draw OH⁻ attacking that carbon.

4_command_terms.short: Explain here means draw the mechanism, not write sentences.
4_command_terms.why: The markscheme credits features of the drawing, so prose about collisions or rates earns no extra marks.
4_command_terms.avoid: Naming the mechanism only; 14N.3.HL.TZ0.10 reports candidates stating names instead of outlining mechanisms.
4_command_terms.demands: Show how electron pairs move through the reaction, using curly arrows on a drawn mechanism.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per feature: first arrow, second arrow, transition state, products. Capped at 3 for SN1.

5_time_efficiency.short: Four drawing moves, about two minutes.
5_time_efficiency.why: A fixed drawing order stops you missing the charge or Br⁻, parts examiners often report as missing (18N.2.HL.TZ0.9).
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Drawing the other mechanism as well; 03M.2.HL.TZ0.5 reports answers giving both.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No explanation of rates, no 180° perfection, no drawing of Na⁺.

6_data_booklet.short: Nothing here is in the booklet; memorise the drawing.
6_data_booklet.why: Mechanism conventions are a skill, not data, so no table can replace drawing them.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Hunting through the booklet for mechanisms during the paper.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Arrow start and end points and the transition state form are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Rule out carbocations, H-started arrows and Na–O bonds at sight.
7_elimination.why: Each contradicts the one-step electron-pair picture or ionic bonding in sodium compounds, so no analysis is needed.
7_elimination.avoid: Drawing NaOH or NaBr with covalent bonds, which examiners reported here (25M.2.HL.6221.4).

definitely_wrong.rule: Rate depends on both reactants, so this is one step with no intermediate.

definitely_wrong.target: An arrow starting at H of OH⁻
definitely_wrong.rule: The electron pair comes from O, not H.

definitely_wrong.target: A covalent Na–O or Na–Br bond
definitely_wrong.rule: These sodium compounds are ionic.

walkthrough.answer: SN2. Curly arrow from the lone pair or negative charge on O of OH⁻ to the C bonded to Br. Curly arrow from the C–Br bond to Br. Transition state with an overall negative charge and partial bonds to O and Br. Products: CH3CH(OH)C(CH3)3 and Br⁻.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.9 mechanisms of halogenoalkanes; R3.4.2 electron-pair movement; R3.4.3 heterolytic fission shown by curly arrows.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show a tidy primary example. Exams use unfamiliar secondary molecules and mark every arrow's start and end.

trigger_phrases: from lone pair/negative charge on O
trap_boundaries: SN1 given instead of SN2: [3 max] (25M.2.HL.6221.4).
NaBr accepted only if Na⁺ was shown at the start (25M.2.HL.6221.4).
Not penalised: HO and Br away from 180°; arrows drawn in the transition state (25M.2.HL.6221.4).
Older schemes also ask for square brackets and warn against a bond drawn from H (18N.2.HL.TZ0.9, 22M.2.HL.TZ1.5).
Heterolytic fission: one atom receives both electrons, or ions form; descriptions reversed with homolytic: [1 max] (25M.2.HL.6221.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial credit usually comes from the correct idea with loose arrows or an incomplete transition state. Full credit needs exact start and end points, charge, partial bonds and both products.

disguises: A bulky secondary bromide in place of a primary one.
Rate data first: deduce the rate expression, then SN2, then draw it (19N.2.HL.TZ0.3).
Iodide or chloride as the leaving group (22M.2.HL.TZ1.5, 19N.2.HL.TZ0.3).
A definition of heterolytic fission asked beside the mechanism: the C–Br arrow is that fission (25M.2.HL.6221.4).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Whatever the molecule: lone pair to carbon, bond to halogen, charged transition state, two products.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per feature of the mechanism, with a cap if the wrong mechanism is drawn.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip written description and redrawing for a perfect 180° line.

6_data_booklet.hack: Mechanism conventions are NOT in the booklet and must be memorised.

rules: Rate depends on both reactants: no carbocation.
Arrows start at a lone pair, negative charge or bond, never at H of OH⁻.
Do not assume the mechanism from a secondary halogenoalkane alone: both occur, so look for a rate clue.

evidence.note: Four marks: two arrows, transition state, products; SN1 capped at 3.
Low scorers struggled with all parts of the mechanism; covalent NaOH and NaBr and wrong products seen.
Arrows not from the lone pair or charge on O; Br arrow wrongly started from C.
Arrow from H of hydroxide and missing charge or brackets in the transition state.
Same mark pattern on a primary bromide, with square brackets and partial bonds.
Sloppy arrow ends, missing charge and missing Br⁻ reported.
Heterolytic fission tested directly in Paper 1A.
About 56% chose the correct heterolytic fission equation.

cards.difficulty_signal: Curly arrows are the most flagged error in this sub-topic. In 2025 the mechanism discriminated strongly, with low scorers struggling on every part (25M.2.HL.6221.4).

cards.title: Classify the carbon first: tertiary means SN1 and a one-term rate

walkthrough.question:
2-bromo-2-methylbutane, CH3CH2CBr(CH3)2, is warmed with sodium hydroxide solution and an alcohol forms. Which option gives the mechanism and the rate expression?
A. SN2; rate = k[CH3CH2CBr(CH3)2][OH⁻]
B. SN1; rate = k[CH3CH2CBr(CH3)2]
C. SN1; rate = k[CH3CH2CBr(CH3)2][OH⁻]
D. SN2; rate = k[CH3CH2CBr(CH3)2]
walkthrough.key_idea: Tertiary halogenoalkane reacts by SN1, so only it appears in the rate expression.
walkthrough.question_type: SN1 vs SN2: mechanism and rate
walkthrough.careful: Count groups on the C–Br carbon, not total carbons.
procedure: Find the carbon bonded to the halogen.
Count the alkyl groups on that carbon.
Three alkyl groups means tertiary, so SN1.
One alkyl group means primary, so SN2.
SN1: two steps, carbocation, rate uses halogenoalkane only.
SN2: one step, transition state, rate uses both reactants.
tricks: Cross out mismatched pairs first: SN1 with two terms, SN2 with one.
Secondary allows both mechanisms: this rule cannot decide, so use rate or stereochemical clues.
if_lost: How many carbon groups does the bromine-bearing carbon hold?
Would a carbocation on this carbon be relatively stable?
Which species take part in the slowest step?

1_context.short: Warm NaOH with a bromide: classify before reading options.
1_context.why: The structure fixes the mechanism, and the mechanism fixes the rate expression, so one classification answers both columns.
1_context.avoid: Using OH⁻ in the reaction as proof it appears in the rate; in SN1 it reacts after the slow step.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.9: primary SN2, tertiary SN1; distinguish the one-step and two-step routes.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach the two mechanisms separately. The exam pairs mechanism with rate expression, so structure and kinetics must be linked in one move.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Mechanism and rate must match: SN1, halogenoalkane only.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Only the slow step sets the rate. In SN1 that step is C–Br breaking alone, so OH⁻ does not affect the rate.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Adding OH⁻ to an SN1 rate; only about 32% were correct on a similar tertiary rate question (15M.1.HL.TZ1.36).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The right mechanism with the wrong rate scores nothing: one option must fit both columns.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: C has SN1 right but adds [OH⁻]; the correct option keeps only the halogenoalkane, as the SN1 slow step requires.

3_novel_application.short: The long name hides a simple tertiary carbon.
3_novel_application.why: Only substitution at the C–Br carbon matters: two methyls and one ethyl make three alkyl groups, whatever the name suggests.
3_novel_application.avoid: Treating the ethyl as part of the main chain and calling the carbon secondary.
3_novel_application.disguise: An ethyl group and a methyl in the name make the carbon look less substituted.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ignore the name: count carbons directly bonded to the C–Br carbon.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: no command term, one pairing to identify.
4_command_terms.why: One mark depends on one correct pairing, so speed comes from classifying, not writing.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing out the whole mechanism; the option needs only its type.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the option where mechanism and rate expression are both right.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing; both columns must be correct.

5_time_efficiency.short: Classify, then cross out mismatches: under a minute.
5_time_efficiency.why: Checking the pairs removes two options at once, leaving one structural decision.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Looking for rate data; none is given, so no calculation is possible.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip drawing the carbocation or the product.

6_data_booklet.short: Not in the booklet; memorise the class-to-mechanism link.
6_data_booklet.why: The link comes from carbocation stability and crowding, which is reasoning rather than data.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching the booklet for rate expressions.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Primary SN2, tertiary SN1, secondary both; SN1 and SN2 rate expressions. All NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Three options go without calculating: only one pair fits.
7_elimination.why: C and D pair a mechanism with the wrong rate, and A gives SN2 to a tertiary carbon.
7_elimination.avoid: Treating C as safe because it says SN1; check its rate too.

definitely_wrong.rule: An SN1 rate cannot include [OH⁻]; OH⁻ joins after the slow step.
An SN2 rate must include both reactants.
A tertiary carbon reacts by SN1, not SN2.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.9 SN1 and SN2 by halogenoalkane class; R3.4.10 leaving group effect on rate.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books describe each mechanism alone. Exams ask which features belong together: steps, intermediate, rate and class.

trigger_phrases: two molecules in the rate-determining step (SN2)
trap_boundaries: SN2 has no intermediate carbocation and one step (25N.1A.HL.6207.40).
SN2 does not replace a nucleophile with an electrophile: a nucleophile replaces the leaving group (25N.1A.HL.6207.40).
Leaving group answers need bond strength or leaving ability; electronegativity was an irrelevant answer (25M.2.HL.6221.4).
Comparison of SN1 and SN2 was hard when similarities were asked: both break a bond heterolytically (18M.2.HL.TZ1.7).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial knowledge names the mechanism. Full credit links the class to steps, intermediate and rate expression.

disguises: A long name hiding a tertiary carbon.
Rate data with no named mechanism (19N.2.HL.TZ0.3).
Comparing iodo and bromo compounds for rate (16N.2.HL.TZ0.6, 21N.2.SL.TZ0.4).
Factors affecting SN1 rate such as branching and leaving group (24M.1.HL.TZ1.35).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Slow step decides everything: one species in it means SN1, two means SN2.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ is all or nothing; written parts give marks per feature named or linked.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not draw the mechanism for an MCQ.

6_data_booklet.hack: Class-to-mechanism link and rate expressions are NOT in the booklet and must be memorised.

rules: SN1 with [OH⁻] in the rate is wrong for one mechanism alone.
SN2 with a one-term rate is wrong.
Tertiary rules out SN2 at this level. Exception: secondary halogenoalkanes use both, so this rule cannot decide them.

evidence.note: Answer B; tertiary bromide, SN1, one-term rate.
Just over 60% correct.
About 32% correct; tertiary SN1 rate depends only on the halogenoalkane.
Answer A; SN2 features tested as statements.
Primary and tertiary compared by order, rate dependence, steps and intermediate; C–Br weaker than C–Cl.
Rate expression deduced, then SN2 stated.
Trouble with leaving group and branching effects on SN1 rate.
C–I weaker than C–Br or I a better leaving group accepted.

cards.difficulty_signal: 60% correct in November 2024 and about 32% in May 2015 on tertiary rate questions.

cards.title: Name the role from the electrons: a pair donor is nucleophile and Lewis base

walkthrough.question:
1-chloropropane is treated with excess potassium cyanide in ethanol: C3H7Cl + KCN → C3H7CN + KCl. What role does the cyanide ion play?
A. Electrophile and Lewis base
B. Nucleophile and Lewis acid
C. Electrophile and Lewis acid
D. Nucleophile and Lewis base
walkthrough.key_idea: A lone-pair donor is both a nucleophile and a Lewis base.
walkthrough.question_type: Identify role: nucleophile, electrophile, Lewis acid or base
walkthrough.careful: Donates a pair, not one electron.
procedure: Find the new bond in the product.
Decide which species supplies both bonding electrons.
Electron-pair donor: call it nucleophile and Lewis base.
Electron-pair acceptor: call it electrophile and Lewis acid.
tricks: Nucleophile always pairs with Lewis base; electrophile always with Lewis acid.
Anion attacking carbon: expect a nucleophile. Neutral lone-pair species also qualify.
if_lost: Which bond is new in C3H7CN?
Which species brought the electrons for that new bond?
Does that species give or receive an electron pair?

1_context.short: CN⁻ attacks the C–Cl carbon and forms the new bond.
1_context.why: The carbon in C–Cl is electron-poor, so the anion's lone pair forms the new C–C bond as chloride leaves.
1_context.avoid: Thinking K⁺ takes part; it is a spectator ion.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.7: nucleophiles are Lewis bases and electrophiles are Lewis acids.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books often teach nucleophiles and Lewis bases in separate places. The exam tests both labels at once on one species.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Two labels, one fact: donating an electron pair.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Both labels describe the same act, so a correct option must use matching labels.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Saying donates an electron; 18N.2.HL.TZ0.9 reports this as the typical slip.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: One electron is not enough: the definition needs a pair.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B has nucleophile right but Lewis acid wrong; the correct option keeps both labels on the donor side.

3_novel_application.short: An organic equation hides a Lewis acid–base question.
3_novel_application.why: The definition concerns only electron pairs, so it applies to organic substitution as well as inorganic reactions.
3_novel_application.avoid: Reading base as Brønsted–Lowry; that is assumed only when Lewis is not specified (16M.1.HL.TZ0.35).
3_novel_application.disguise: A substitution equation with KCN replaces the usual inorganic Lewis example.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ignore context: ask who donates the electron pair to form the new bond.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: both labels must be right.
4_command_terms.why: One mark covers both labels, so half-correct options earn nothing.
4_command_terms.avoid: Stopping at nucleophile and picking the first option containing it.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the option with both labels correct for CN⁻.

5_time_efficiency.short: Spot the donor, pair the labels: twenty seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: Because the labels must pair, identifying one settles the other.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Working through the reaction mechanism; it is not needed.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the mechanism, solvent and excess KCN details.

6_data_booklet.short: Definitions are not in the booklet; memorise the pairing.
6_data_booklet.why: These are definitions, not data, so no table can replace them.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking in the booklet for acid–base definitions.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Lewis acid accepts a pair; Lewis base donates a pair; nucleophile = Lewis base. All NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Mixed labels and electrophile options can be cut immediately.
7_elimination.why: Electrophile with Lewis base, or nucleophile with Lewis acid, are contradictions. An anion donating a lone pair cannot be the acceptor here.
7_elimination.avoid: Placing the donating lone pair on N; drawn arrows must start at carbon of CN⁻ (14M.3.SL.TZ1.22, 15N.3.HL.TZ0.33).

definitely_wrong.rule: An electrophile accepts a pair, so it cannot be a Lewis base.
A nucleophile donates a pair, so it cannot be a Lewis acid.
CN⁻ donates its lone pair here; it does not accept one.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.1 nucleophiles; R3.4.6 Lewis acid and base; R3.4.7 nucleophiles are Lewis bases.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books separate organic and acid–base language. Exams merge them on one species.

trap_boundaries: Base means Brønsted–Lowry unless Lewis is specified (16M.1.HL.TZ0.35).
Typical error: donating an electron rather than a pair (18N.2.HL.TZ0.9).
Explaining the role can be scored by naming the nucleophile, the lone pair or attack on the partially positive carbon (21N.2.SL.TZ0.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial answers say donates electrons. Full answers say an electron pair and name the matching role.

disguises: Substitution equations with KCN.
Water in a Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis comparison (21N.2.HL.TZ0.5).
A short role question beside a mechanism (18N.2.HL.TZ0.9).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Follow the new bond back to the species that supplied both electrons.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ is all or nothing; written definitions earn one mark for the electron-pair statement.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No mechanism and no equation balancing.

6_data_booklet.hack: Definitions are NOT in the booklet and must be memorised.

rules: Electrophile with Lewis base is a contradiction.
Nucleophile with Lewis acid is a contradiction.
Anions are donors, but do not assume all donors are anions: neutral species can be nucleophiles (R3.4.1).

evidence.note: Answer D for CN⁻.
Lewis base donates a pair of electrons.
Typical error was donating an electron.
Nucleophile/Lewis base and lone pair credited.
Lewis base role given as electron pair donor/nucleophile.
Base read as Brønsted–Lowry unless Lewis is specified.
Arrow wrongly drawn from N of the nitrile group instead of C.
Arrow wrongly from N of CN⁻ instead of C.

cards.difficulty_signal: Examiners report this as generally done well (November 2018), but the 'electron not pair' slip recurs. No 2025 percentage in the pack.

cards.title: Benzene's electron-rich ring needs an electron-poor cation, not an anion

walkthrough.question:
Benzene undergoes a substitution reaction with an ion. Which ion could act as the attacking species?
A. NO2⁻
B. NH4⁺
C. NO2⁺
D. Br⁻
walkthrough.key_idea: Benzene's delocalized electrons attack an electron-poor cation, the electrophile.
walkthrough.careful: A positive charge alone is not enough; check for room.
procedure: Recall benzene's ring has high electron density.
So it reacts with electrophiles, not nucleophiles.
Rule out anions; electrophiles accept electron pairs.
Among cations, check the centre can accept a pair.
tricks: Pick the cation that can accept a pair. Fails for NH4⁺: N has no room.
Reaction name tells you the partner: electrophilic substitution needs an electrophile.
if_lost: Is the benzene ring rich or poor in electrons?
So would it attract positive or negative species?
Which ions here have a centre able to accept an electron pair?

1_context.short: Benzene reacts by electrophilic substitution, so it needs an electrophile.
1_context.why: The delocalized pi cloud is electron-rich, so it attracts an electron-poor partner and repels anions.
1_context.avoid: Thinking any ion suits benzene; only about 36% found the right species (25M.1A.HL.6219.40).
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.13: benzene reacts with a charged electrophile, E⁺, by electrophilic substitution.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach nitration with mixed acids and a long mechanism. This question asks only which ion is the electrophile, with no reagents given.

2_markscheme_logic.short: The mark goes to recognising NO2⁺ as the electrophile.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Only NO2⁺ has a positive nitrogen able to accept a pair from the ring, which starts the mechanism.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Confusing NO2⁺ with NO2⁻; one charge changes the answer.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The charge sign decides it: NO2⁻ and NO2⁺ share atoms but not the role.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A has the same atoms as the correct option, but its negative charge means the ring repels it.

3_novel_application.short: Four ions test one idea: who accepts electrons.
3_novel_application.why: Whatever the ion, the ring donates the pair, so the partner must be able to accept it.
3_novel_application.avoid: Treating NH4⁺ as suitable just because it is a cation.
3_novel_application.disguise: No mention of electrophile or nitration; only the word substitution.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Benzene substitution? Ask which species is electron-poor with room for a pair.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: no command term, choose one ion.
4_command_terms.why: A single mark rewards recognising the electrophile; no mechanism need be drawn.
4_command_terms.avoid: Trying to write the full nitration route.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the one ion that can attack benzene.

5_time_efficiency.short: Charge check, then room check: about twenty seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: The sign rule removes anions instantly; the remaining cation comparison takes one look.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Recalling mixed-acid reagents; forming the electrophile is not assessed (R3.4.13).
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip mixed-acid equations and mechanism steps.

6_data_booklet.short: Not in the booklet; memorise benzene's electrophile behaviour.
6_data_booklet.why: Electrophile identity is reaction knowledge, not a data table entry.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching the booklet for reacting species.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution; NO2⁺ acts as an electrophile. NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Both anions go at once; NH4⁺ goes on the room check.
7_elimination.why: The electron-rich ring repels anions, and ammonium's nitrogen has a full octet with no lone pair.
7_elimination.avoid: Assuming every cation is an electrophile.

definitely_wrong.rule: An anion is repelled by the electron-rich ring.
An anion is repelled by the electron-rich ring.
N has a full octet, so it cannot accept a pair.

walkthrough.answer: C. NO2⁺, which acts as the electrophile.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.4 electrophiles accept both bonding electrons; R3.4.13 benzene with E⁺.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books bury the electrophile in nitration conditions. Exams isolate it as a single choice of species.

trap_boundaries: Cl⁺ is correct where Cl2, Cl• and Cl⁻ are offered (25M.1A.HL.6207.40).
A high-electron-density answer needs the link to attraction of electrophiles or repulsion of nucleophiles (21N.2.HL.TZ0.10).
Electrophilic and nucleophilic substitution are often confused (13M.3.HL.TZ2.2).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial knowledge says benzene is reactive. Full credit links the electron-rich ring to an electron-poor attacker.

disguises: Only ions listed, without the word electrophile.
Halogen species as Cl2, Cl•, Cl⁺, Cl⁻ (25M.1A.HL.6207.40).
Explain why benzene does not react with nucleophiles (21N.2.HL.TZ0.10).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Rich ring needs a poor partner: cation with room for a pair.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ is all or nothing; written explanations score electron density and the attraction or repulsion that follows.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not recall how the electrophile forms: it is not assessed in R3.4.13.

6_data_booklet.hack: Electrophile identity is NOT in the booklet and must be memorised.

rules: Anions cannot be the electrophile attacking benzene.
Radicals are not the charged electrophile E⁺ of R3.4.13.
Do not rule out neutral species in general: electrophiles can be neutral (R3.4.4).

evidence.note: Answer C.
About 36% identified NO2⁺ as a species attacking benzene.
Answer C (Cl⁺) in the same pattern.
Delocalized electrons, high electron density, electrophiles attracted, nucleophiles repelled.
Arrow from ring to N of NO2⁺ in the mechanism.
Confusion of electrophilic and nucleophilic substitution.

cards.difficulty_signal: About 36% correct in May 2025 (25M.1A.HL.6219.40). Examiners also list this among difficult areas that session.

cards.title: Benzene's structure: sort evidence into chemical and physical, and say C to C

walkthrough.question: Styrene, C8H8, can be drawn two ways. Structure A shows the ring with a circle inside it. Structure B shows the ring with alternating single and double bonds. Give one chemical reason and one physical reason why Structure A represents a benzene ring better. [2]
walkthrough.key_idea: Chemical means how it reacts; physical means measured structure: equal C–C lengths.
walkthrough.question_type: Benzene: evidence against alternating double bonds
walkthrough.careful: Keep categories straight: reversed reasons earn only one mark.
procedure: Read which category each answer line wants.
Chemical: give a reaction behaviour, such as substitution over addition.
Physical: give a measured structural fact about the ring.
Write C–C bonds explicitly, not just bonds.
tricks: Chemical answers describe reacting; physical answers need a length or angle.
Hydrogenation enthalpy counts as chemical here: less exothermic than three times cyclohexene.
if_lost: What would alternating double bonds make benzene do with most reagents?
What would you measure in a ring with alternating single and double bonds?
Which of your ideas describes reacting, and which describes measuring?

1_context.short: Compare circle and alternating bonds as models of benzene.
1_context.why: The circle means delocalized pi electrons, so reactivity and bond measurements should differ from those of three separate double bonds.
1_context.avoid: Giving only one category; the question needs one of each.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.13: benzene reacts with electrophiles by substitution, the chemical evidence for delocalization.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books list evidence in one paragraph. The exam separates chemical from physical and penalises a swap.

2_markscheme_logic.short: One mark each: a chemical property and a physical property.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Each line is marked separately, so a true fact in the wrong line loses credit.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Writing bond lengths as chemical evidence; examiners report this confusion (17M.2.HL.TZ1.7).
trigger_phrases: all bond angles the same / planar
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Reasons reversed: [1 max]. A 2017 report rejected bond lengths not stated as C to C.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Two marks need the right fact in the right line; reversing them scores only one.

3_novel_application.short: Styrene looks new, but the question is about the ring.
3_novel_application.why: Styrene's side chain has a normal double bond, so your reasons must describe the ring, not the whole molecule.
3_novel_application.avoid: Saying styrene does not add; its side chain can, as its polymerisation shows.
3_novel_application.disguise: Styrene replaces benzene, and its side C=C could distract from the ring.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Cover the side chain; answer for the ring alone.

4_command_terms.short: State: brief facts, no explanation needed.
4_command_terms.why: State rewards specific brief answers, so each line needs one fact only.
4_command_terms.avoid: Explaining delocalization at length for no extra mark.
4_command_terms.demands: One brief chemical fact and one brief physical fact about benzene.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per category; [1 max] if the two are swapped.

5_time_efficiency.short: Two short lines, about forty seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: A memorised pair answers this family instantly, leaving time for harder parts.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing several reasons per line; extra facts add no marks.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip drawing resonance forms and explaining orbital overlap.

6_data_booklet.short: Not in the booklet; memorise one reason of each type.
6_data_booklet.why: These reasons are learnt facts about benzene, so no table replaces them.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Hunting for a data table to justify a State answer.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Substitution over addition; equal C–C lengths and angles; planar. All NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Rule out formula facts and anything true of both models.
7_elimination.why: Evidence counts only if it separates the two models; facts shared by both disprove nothing.
7_elimination.avoid: Saying benzene is unsaturated or C6H6; both fit the alternating model (25M.1A.HL.6207.13).

definitely_wrong.rule: Both structures have the same formula.

definitely_wrong.target: Simply that it can be hydrogenated
definitely_wrong.rule: Both models can add hydrogen. Only the enthalpy of hydrogenation separates them.

definitely_wrong.target: Bond lengths in the chemical line
definitely_wrong.rule: A length is measured, so it is physical.

walkthrough.answer: Chemical (any one): does not easily undergo addition; undergoes electrophilic substitution; hydrogenation enthalpy less exothermic than three times cyclohexene; all C–C bond energies the same. Physical (any one): all bond lengths the same; all bond angles the same or molecule planar.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.13 benzene substitution, which rests on the delocalized ring.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books present evidence as a single list. Exams ask for labelled categories and for facts that truly separate the models.

trap_boundaries: Properties reversed: [1 max] (25N.2.HL.6209.2).
'All bond lengths are equal' without C to C did not score in 2017 (17M.2.HL.TZ1.7), though the 2025 scheme words it more loosely: always write C–C.
Do not offer C6H6, unsaturation or hydrogenation alone as disproof (25M.1A.HL.6207.13).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial credit: one correct fact or a swap. Full credit: one correctly placed fact in each category.

disguises: A benzene derivative such as styrene.
Kekulé's structure and a disproving fact (25M.1A.HL.6207.13).
Bond enthalpy or hydrogenation data as evidence (18M.2.SL.TZ1.3).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Would the alternating model predict something different? Only then is it evidence.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per correctly categorised fact.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No orbital explanation unless the circle is asked about separately.

6_data_booklet.hack: The evidence list is NOT in the booklet and must be memorised.

rules: Formula and unsaturation fit both models.
Hydrogenation alone fits both models; only its enthalpy separates them.
A measured length or angle is physical, never chemical.

evidence.note: Chemical and physical reasons listed, one mark each, [1 max] if reversed.
Answer C: equal C–C lengths disprove the alternating structure.
Few distinguished physical from chemical; lengths without C to C did not score.
Very few correct; same confusion and lengths not specified as between carbons.
Physical given instead of chemical evidence lost the mark.
Equal C–C bonds and intermediate bond character credited.

cards.difficulty_signal: Examiners repeatedly flag physical vs chemical confusion and unspecified bond lengths (2014, 2017).

cards.title: Major product: earn the mark with carbocation stability, not Markovnikov's name

walkthrough.question: But-1-ene reacts with HBr, giving two structural isomers of bromobutane. Explain which isomer is the major product. [2]
walkthrough.key_idea: The major product comes from the more stable carbocation: more alkyl groups.
walkthrough.question_type: Unsymmetrical alkene: predict and explain major product
walkthrough.careful: Never stop at Markovnikov's rule; compare the carbocations.
procedure: Draw both carbocations from H adding to either C=C carbon.
Count alkyl groups on each positive carbon.
More alkyl groups means more stable carbocation.
Put the halide on that positive carbon for the product.
Give the reason: alkyl groups release electrons, stabilising C⁺.
tricks: Compare the two carbocations actually formed; tertiary versus secondary also appears.
Markovnikov predicts quickly, but write carbocation stability. Fails for credit if stated alone.
if_lost: What intermediate forms when H⁺ adds to the double bond?
Which two positions could the positive charge occupy?
How many alkyl groups does each positive carbon hold?

1_context.short: But-1-ene is unsymmetrical, so two carbocations are possible.
1_context.why: H can add to either alkene carbon and the charge lands on the other, giving primary or secondary carbocations.
1_context.avoid: Considering only one carbocation; the comparison is what the second mark rewards.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.12: relative carbocation stability explains the major product with unsymmetrical alkenes.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books often offer Markovnikov's rule as the reason. Markschemes reward the carbocation stability behind it and give nothing for the rule itself.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Two marks: name the isomer, then justify with carbocation stability.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The rule predicts the product but gives no cause, and Explain requires the cause.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Quoting Markovnikov's rule alone; no M2 here, and 15M.3.SL.TZ1.20 reports many losing marks this way.
trigger_phrases: secondary carbocation more stable than primary
alkyl groups electron releasing / greater inductive effect
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Stating Markovnikov's rule alone earns no M2.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: One mark for the isomer; the second needs a stated carbocation comparison or alkyl-group effect.

3_novel_application.short: Different alkene, same test: compare the two carbocations.
3_novel_application.why: The comparison depends on the carbocations actually formed, so a branched alkene may pit tertiary against secondary.
3_novel_application.avoid: Using secondary versus primary by habit; 15N.3.HL.TZ0.34 reports this error on a tertiary example.
3_novel_application.disguise: Later versions swap HBr for HI or water, or use a branched alkene.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Whatever adds, H goes on first: which resulting carbocation has more alkyl groups?

4_command_terms.short: Explain: state the isomer and give the cause.
4_command_terms.why: Explain asks for reasons, so the product alone reaches only half the marks.
4_command_terms.avoid: Giving the product with no reason.
4_command_terms.demands: Identify the major isomer and give the reason based on carbocation stability.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for the isomer, one for the reason.

5_time_efficiency.short: Two sentences: isomer, then reason; under a minute.
5_time_efficiency.why: Both marks come from one comparison, so no mechanism is needed in this answer.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Drawing curly arrows here; they earn nothing for this explanation.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip mechanism arrows and Markovnikov's wording.

6_data_booklet.short: Not in the booklet; memorise the carbocation stability order.
6_data_booklet.why: The order is reasoning from inductive effects, so no table supplies it.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching the booklet for carbocation data.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Tertiary more stable than secondary, secondary more stable than primary, because alkyl groups release electrons. NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Rule out Markovnikov-only answers and the primary-carbocation product.
7_elimination.why: A primary carbocation has fewer electron-releasing groups, so its product is minor; the rule alone states no cause.
7_elimination.avoid: Naming 1-bromobutane because the chain looks simpler.

definitely_wrong.rule: It needs the less stable primary carbocation.

definitely_wrong.target: A reason quoting only Markovnikov's rule
definitely_wrong.rule: No cause is given, so M2 is not awarded.
One HBr adds one Br across one C=C.

walkthrough.answer: 2-bromobutane, CH3CHBrCH2CH3. It forms through a secondary carbocation, which is more stable than the primary one because alkyl groups release electrons.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.5 high electron density of C=C; R3.4.11 mechanisms; R3.4.12 carbocation stability and major product.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach Markovnikov's rule as a shortcut. Exams give no mark for it alone.

trigger_phrases: arrow from C=C to H of HBr
arrow from lone pair/negative charge on Br⁻ to C⁺
trap_boundaries: Markovnikov's rule alone: no M2 (24N.2.HL.TZ0.2).
A mechanism giving the wrong isomer is not penalised if that isomer was the earlier answer (24N.2.HL.TZ0.2).
Why alkenes react: 'presence of C=C' alone is not accepted; say high electron density (25N.2.HL.6221.4).
Mechanism marks: arrow from C=C to H with H–Br fission, carbocation, arrow from Br⁻ to C⁺ (16N.2.HL.TZ0.5, 21M.2.HL.TZ1.5).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial credit names the isomer. Full credit compares carbocations or explains the alkyl-group effect.

disguises: Branched alkene with tertiary vs secondary (21M.2.HL.TZ2.4, 15N.3.HL.TZ0.34).
Other hydrogen halides such as HI (21N.2.HL.TZ0.10).
Propene with HCl (19N.2.HL.TZ0.3).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Write both carbocations, then let alkyl count decide.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Product mark plus reason mark; mechanism parts are marked per arrow and carbocation.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No rule quotation and no mechanism unless asked.

6_data_booklet.hack: Carbocation order is NOT in the booklet and must be memorised.

rules: The product from the less substituted carbocation is the minor one.
A reason quoting only Markovnikov's rule is not enough.
Symmetrical alkenes give one product, so this comparison does not apply to them.

evidence.note: 2-bromobutane, secondary carbocation reason, no M2 for the rule alone.
Most attributed the product to carbocation stability.
Most simply stated Markovnikov's rule and scored nothing on that part.
Stability stated without the electron-releasing alkyl explanation lost the mark.
Compared secondary with primary instead of tertiary with secondary.
Secondary vs primary carbocation and inductive effect credited.
High electron density required; presence of C=C alone rejected.

cards.difficulty_signal: Mean 1.28/2 in November 2024 (24N.2.HL.TZ0.2). Examiners repeatedly report rule-only answers as scoring nothing.

cards.title: Optical isomers of a halogenoalkane: mirror the wedge-dash drawing

walkthrough.question: The bromoalkane CH3CHBrC(CH3)3 contains a chiral carbon. Draw its two optical isomers so that the three-dimensional arrangement around that carbon is clear. [2]
walkthrough.key_idea: Draw one 3-D isomer, then its exact mirror image, keeping tetrahedral angles.
walkthrough.careful: Swapping groups and wedges together makes identical drawings.
procedure: Find the carbon with four different groups.
Draw it with two plain bonds, one wedge, one dash.
Keep angles tetrahedral, not 90°.
Draw a mirror line and reflect every group.
Check the two drawings do not superimpose.
tricks: Mirror it, never swap and flip: two changes recreate the same molecule.
Check the C(CH3)3 carbon: three identical methyls, so it is not chiral.
if_lost: Which carbon holds four different groups?
How do wedge and dash bonds show three dimensions?
What would a mirror do to each group's position?

1_context.short: The chiral carbon carries H, Br, CH3 and C(CH3)3.
1_context.why: Four different groups make the carbon chiral, so the molecule and its mirror image cannot be superimposed.
1_context.avoid: Missing the chiral centre, which examiners report here (25M.2.HL.6221.4).
1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.9: the stereospecific nature of SN2 should be covered, which needs 3-D drawings.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach chirality in a structure chapter. Exams set it on the same molecule as substitution, where SN2 inversion needs the same wedge-dash skill.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Two 3-D mirror images earn both marks; flat drawings cap at one.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The cap separates knowing the isomers from showing their geometry, which only wedge and dash can show.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: 90° bond angles or no wedge-dash, both reported here (25M.2.HL.6221.4).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Non-3-D with correct angles: [1 max]. Bond angles of 90°: not accepted.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: One mark: two isomers with correct angles but flat. Both marks: wedge-dash shown on both isomers.

3_novel_application.short: The bulky group is just one more label on the carbon.
3_novel_application.why: Chirality depends on four different groups, not on their size, so C(CH3)3 counts as one group.
3_novel_application.avoid: Drawing every methyl in 3-D; only the chiral carbon needs it.
3_novel_application.disguise: A bulky C(CH3)3 group makes the chiral centre harder to spot.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Scan for a carbon with four different attachments; treat each attachment as one block.

4_command_terms.short: Draw: accurate geometry is what gets marked.
4_command_terms.why: Draw requires an accurate representation, so angles and 3-D notation are what is marked.
4_command_terms.demands: Show both isomers, with wedge and dash around the chiral carbon.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Two marks; [1 max] for flat drawings with correct angles.

5_time_efficiency.short: Copy, reflect, check: about a minute.
5_time_efficiency.why: Reflecting the first drawing needs no new thinking and prevents the swap error.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Redrawing the second isomer from scratch, which invites errors.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip explaining optical rotation; it is not asked.

6_data_booklet.short: Not in the booklet; memorise the drawing convention.
6_data_booklet.why: Wedge-dash is a convention, not data, so no table supplies it.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for a structure template in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Wedge-dash convention and the four-different-groups test are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Reject 90° drawings and pairs that superimpose.
7_elimination.why: A 90° cross misrepresents a tetrahedral carbon, and superimposable drawings are one molecule, not two isomers.
7_elimination.avoid: Swapping two groups as well as wedge and dash, which recreates the same molecule (25M.2.HL.6221.4).

definitely_wrong.rule: Not accepted by the markscheme.
Superimposable drawings are not two isomers.

definitely_wrong.target: Choosing the C(CH3)3 carbon as chiral
definitely_wrong.rule: Three identical methyl groups rule it out.

walkthrough.answer: Two mirror images around the carbon bonded to H, Br, CH3 and C(CH3)3, each drawn with tetrahedral angles and wedge and dash bonds.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R3.4.9 stereospecific nature of SN2, which depends on 3-D representation.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books separate chirality from mechanisms. Exams place both on one molecule and expect the link.

trap_boundaries: Flat drawings with correct angles: [1 max] (25M.2.HL.6221.4).
Bond angles of 90° not accepted (25M.2.HL.6221.4).
SN2 gives inversion; SN1 gives about 50% of each, so a mix suggests both mechanisms (16N.2.HL.TZ0.6, 18M.2.HL.TZ2.9).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial credit shows the isomers. Full credit shows true 3-D geometry and a real mirror relationship.

disguises: A bulky group near the chiral carbon.
Asking for the outcome at a chiral carbon: inversion vs near-equal mixture (16N.2.HL.TZ0.6).
Planar carbocation attacked from either side (18M.2.HL.TZ2.9).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Find four different blocks, then mirror them; for mechanisms, ask if attack comes from one side or both.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Drawings are capped when 3-D is missing; explanation parts score per mechanism outcome.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not draw every methyl in 3-D.

6_data_booklet.hack: Wedge-dash and chirality rules are NOT in the booklet and must be memorised.

rules: A carbon with two identical groups is not chiral.
90° angles are not accepted.
Identical drawings are not optical isomers: check by mirror line, since one swap alone inverts, but a swap plus wedge-dash change restores.

evidence.note: [1 max] without 3-D; 90° angles rejected.
About half correct; missing chiral centre, 90° angles, no wedge-dash, swaps giving identical drawings.
Mirror image; SN2 inversion and SN1 near 50% of each.
Planar carbocation attacked from either side, about 50% each.
SN2 inversion contrasted with about 50:50 for SN1.

cards.difficulty_signal: About half drew these correctly in May 2025 (25M.2.HL.6221.4). 'Inversion caused by SN1 and SN2' listed as difficult in November 2016.
